en: Composed by the Tang Dynasty Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhànrán.
Commentary on the "Chapter on the Dharma Master.
This commentary on the chapter is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed explanation. The initial section has two parts; first—
Regarding the explanation of the five Dharma Masters, this follows the sequential reduction of the number.
This section further has two parts:

first, citing sūtras and śāstras to distinguish between their combination or separation, and their existence or non-existence; second, determining the general and specific aspects to conclude the title of the chapter.
The first section has two parts:
first, based on the present sutra, the five [types] are categorized; second, from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* onwards, alternative explanations for the names are presented.

By comparing them with the present [sutra], one distinguishes their combinations, separations, presences, and absences, even proceeding as below to explain them by reducing the number; thus, whether many or few, they are all termed "Dharma-preachers."

Regarding the first five types of Dharma-preachers, there is not a single word in the text concerning the terms "one" or "two," etc.; rather, they have been collectively established by both ancient and modern scholars as the "five kinds of Dharma-preachers.
Since the number established in the sūtras and śāstras varies, this chapter simply refers to them generically as "Dharma-preachers."
The *Devarāja-prajñā* states:
"There are ten dharmas for receiving and upholding this sūtra:

first, transcribing; second, making offerings; third, circulating; fourth, listening attentively; fifth, reading for oneself; sixth, memorizing; seventh, explaining extensively; eighth, reciting; ninth, reflecting; and tenth, practicing."

Among the ten [sections], the first is the fifth in the current text; the fourth and sixth are the first in the current text; the fifth is the second; the eighth is the third; the seventh is the fourth; these are circulated and included within the "Extensive Explanation" (廣說) section; the remaining three are all included within the "Recollection and Retention" (憶持) section.

In that sutra, "recollection" (*smṛti*) is merely "reception" (*vedanā*); in the *Mahā-śāstra*, reception and upholding (*dhāraṇā*) are divided into two, so one should not speak of them simply as "recollection and upholding.

This "Separate Treatise" below judges the general and the specific to conclude the title of the chapter; therein, it first distinguishes between self and other to differentiate the stages of the teacher.

Regarding the statement, "The Great Sūtra is divided into nine sections," and so forth, this was originally a distinct interpretation; however, it is here borrowed for the purpose of corroborating the five kinds of Dharma-preachers.
These nine sections consist of the *Hiraṇyavatī* and eight *Gaṅgā* rivers. The fourth *Gaṅgā* is explained extensively, wherein the meaning of one part out of sixteen divisions is elucidated.

Regarding the statement, "The first four have no understanding," it means that in the third *gaṅgā*, one understands three parts; in the fifth *gaṅgā*, eight parts; in the sixth *gaṅgā*, twelve parts; and in the seventh *gaṅgā*, fourteen parts. In the eighth *gaṅgā*, one fully understands the meaning in its entirety. Therefore, one must proceed from being able to understand even a single part of the meaning; to be able to explain it to others is the stage of a teacher (*ācārya*).

Next, in the "General Discussion" (*sāmānyanirdeśa*), we set aside the specific for the general; thus, both self and others may equally receive this title of the chapter. From the perspective of its general meaning, there is not a single sentence that is unfit to serve as a teacher.
Next, the explanation by way of reducing the numbers consists of four parts:
namely, four, three, two, and one. These are all successive condensations of the many into the few, none of which deviates from the Dharma Master’s intent.
As for the phrase "as explained below," it refers in full to the initial explanation of the four practices in the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (*Anle-xing-pin*).

Since the "four" refer to those [previous categories], this section should likewise employ the "four" to conclude the title of the chapter; their absence in the text is due to abbreviation, as can be understood from the examples provided at the beginning, end, and middle.
If one wishes to know [the full title], it is simply that one first distinguishes between the general and the specific, and then concludes the chapter title based on the general four.
The four sections are grouped into three, which further constitute three intentions:

first, the three karmas; second, the three gates; third, the three dharmas. Each of these is first explained individually, followed by a judgment on their common and specific aspects to conclude the title of the chapter.
Next, the three are condensed into two, namely: practicing for oneself and transforming others.

As for the phrase "no longer recording," it may be understood by analogy with what preceded; this is also a prior explanation, followed by a judgment on the common and specific [aspects], thereby concluding the title of the chapter.

Since this applies universally to both self and others across the preceding three [categories], we know that there are both specific and general aspects regarding self and others: specifically, they are distinct from one another; generally, they interpenetrate, because both self and others are mutually capable [of acting as cause and effect].
Now, because this section generally concerns transforming others, it is titled "The Chapter on the Dharma Master. Next, regarding the condensation of two into one:

the statement that "the Tathāgata’s practice encompasses all practices" relies on the text of the "Chapter on Noble Practices" (*Ārya-caryā*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Furthermore, there is one practice that constitutes the Tathāgata’s practice, namely the Mahāyāna Great Parinirvāṇa. Since Nirvāṇa is precisely the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), the text now uses the three—house, clothing, and seat—to explain these three virtues. These three virtues are themselves the single Great Nirvāṇa; this Great Nirvāṇa pervades all places and all phenomena, and is thus collectively termed "one. This is explained first, followed by a reference to the extensive version.
The initial explanation consists of two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific.
Regarding the general: a single practice universally encompasses the three dharmas of the chamber and so forth.
The separate pairings are twofold:
first, the direct pairings; second, the detailed analysis.

The initial section contains nine items, each of which pairs three dharmas with all other dharmas; thus, the first pairing concerns the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the neutral (or "sweeping away") characteristics.
Next, from "Furthermore, loving-kindness and patience" onwards, there are merit and wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "Wisdom is the eye," it should also be said that one who is complete with both eyes and feet must have something upon which to rely; this is because the basis [for these] consists of two things.

Third, from "Furthermore, compassion" onwards, there is a refutation of partiality and deviance; this also first provides an explanation, followed by a citation from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* as proof, showing that superior to partiality and deviance is the courageous cultivation of the Perfect [Teaching].

4. Regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore, compassion," the four māras are refuted; this is also explained first. Within this explanation, one must provide a comprehensive interpretation based on that which lies outside the realms (*dhātu*), followed by citing evidence for emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The phrase "and so forth" explains the underlying meaning. The section beginning with "Furthermore, compassion and...

clarifies the possession of the two adornments (*dvayasaṃbhāra*). This is further explained in two ways, which are merely the reverse of the previous explanation; according to the latter in relation to the former, the preceding [explanation] should have stated "compassion and patience."
6. From "Because of loving-kindness and patience" onwards, the refutation and establishment by means of analogies are fully provided, following the two examples previously mentioned.
7. From "Furthermore, because of compassion, what [is there]... onwards, it concerns essence and function; as for function, it is the very departure from faults.

8. From "The emergence of the three truths" (*tri-satya*) onwards, it is explained according to names; this differs from the sequential three truths, as they are encompassed within the chamber of compassion, the robe of patience, and samādhi.
9. From "The sūtra says" onwards, it cites the sūtra: formlessness (*animitta*) is the seat.

Next, regarding the indication of its breadth, the phrase "cannot be exhausted, etc. means that it is fully explained in the *Xuán* (Mysterious) text as the perfect five practices (*wǔ xíng*) encompassing all practices; it is also like the ten vehicles and ten objects (*shí shèng shí jìng*) in the *Zhǐguān* which comprehensively include them both horizontally and vertically, as well as the horizontal and vertical dharma-gates within the "Pervasive Destruction" (*pò biàn*), and even the four kinds of samādhis which encompass all practices—since all practices are but a single practice, they are explained through these nine texts.
Next, the following section provides a critical analysis of the "Questions.

Regarding the initial question: according to the first explanation of the chapter, it should state "five kinds"; according to the subsequent reduction of the number, it should state "one dharma. Why, then, are only the three—robes, seats, and dwellings—correlated with all dharmas?

The respondent replies: To manifest the principle based on the facts, one must possess three methods; moreover, according to the present text, one should possess these three methods when preaching for the assembly. Therefore, it is only when the three aspects of fact, principle, and their integration are complete that one may preach the Dharma. Thus, first is the explanation of the facts, second is the synthesis of fact and principle, and third is the exclusive application of principle.
The explanation of the details follows the text.

Regarding the mention of "three gates" in the combined interpretation: the first two belong to the phenomenal (factual) realm, while the last one belongs to the noumenal (principle) realm; both phenomenon and principle are objects of delusion.
First, regarding "in terms of the fruit of suffering," the gate of compassion is employed because suffering must be uprooted.
Next, regarding "in terms of fetters and karma," the gate of patience is employed because one departs from them in accordance with principle.
Third, "in terms of the objects of the truths," one employs the gate of emptiness because of dwelling well in emptiness.

Third, "singly in terms of principle": since principle is the principle of the truths, one relies on the three truths; this is because the preceding third [section] already possesses all three truths.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yún yún*), one should explain these three by correlating them with various sets of three dharmas, thereby making them perfectly integrated, harmonious, and unimpeded; only then will one understand that this text encompasses the universal characteristics of the teachings. Therefore, the text below summarizes the teaching by stating: "In general, wherever there are multiple explanations of a chapter, they all pertain to the Perfect Teaching (*yánjiào*)."
Next, the section beginning with "As for 'Dharma'" provides a specific explanation.

The two characters "Dharma-master" (fǎshī) pervade all the preceding explanations, as the aforementioned dharmas constitute the teacher’s dharma; therefore, the current explanation of the name is also categorized according to two kinds, up to five kinds.

Regarding the explanation through the causes and conditions of "if oneself," etc.: first, the distinction between self and others is the worldly [truth], which refers to following one's own precepts to instruct others.

The accomplishment of one's own practice is the generation of goodness; transforming others to eliminate evil is the remedial [truth]. That both self and others are called "Dharma Masters" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The phrase "all the various types" below refers to the classification of teachings (*jiao*); as with the various types mentioned previously, it cannot be explained otherwise.
"Qiá" (洽) means "moistening.
The term "external ordinary person" (*wàifán*) will be explained in its proper context in the main text that follows.
If that is so, how does this differ from the former? Answer:

It differs because it clarifies [the path] for the sake of both oneself and others; because it is distinct from the Śrāvakas; because one’s own practice is free from anxiety, exclusion, and humiliation; and because one’s benefit to others is free from contempt, lack of power, and weakness. Only the single aspect of "retrogression" resembles the former, which is why it is said, "not necessarily."

Regarding the statement from "outer ordinary beings" (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) to "not worrying about perilous suffering": the five grades of outer ordinary beings rejoice in the merit of widespread propagation; however, the Śrāvakas are single-mindedly intent on severing the mind that benefits others. When they hear that the Mahāsattvas have been expelled by the multitude, they reflect that their own power of contemplation is not yet profound. If they do not rely [on the Bodhisattvas], they will internally defile their pure contemplation and externally invite derision, thereby failing in the way of benefiting others. Therefore, the Buddha taught the Four Practices of Peaceful Happiness (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*) to prevent such afflictions. Because they distance themselves from those ten provocations (*daśa-kṣobha*), it is said "they do not worry."

Regarding the phrase "both to testify and to assist": the jeweled stūpa comes to testify to the sutra, and the emanated bodies assemble to assist in its exposition; through this testimony and assistance, they inspire the aspiration for its widespread circulation.
Regarding the phrase "further demonstrating the method for mastering the sūtra," the three practices beginning with donning the robe are as explained below.
Regarding the phrase "thereupon addressed," etc., it originally relied upon Bhaisajyarāja; from this point, it was addressed to others—this constitutes the propagation.
Regarding the initial statement, "First he addressed eighty thousand great beings," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The Lotus Sūtra is a secret entrusted to the bodhisattvas. As indicated by the subsequent passage where he summons those from the lower regions, it appears that even they must await their original retinues to verify whether others are yet capable.

Regarding "General and Specific Predictions": "General" refers to the prediction of seven hundred [kalpas], while "Specific" refers to the prediction of kalpas, lands, and so forth. The character "絓" (huà) is pronounced as in "卦" (guà); it means to suppress or to anticipate.
Regarding the phrase "even for a single thought-moment" and so forth, this clarifies that by means of this very thought, one will certainly attain bodhi.
Since the remote cause does not perish but rather relies upon this [thought] to manifest, it is distinguished from other forms of merit.

To investigate this thoroughly, one must fully practice the path and teachings of all Buddhas; even for those of the Two Vehicles who have received their predictions, they still require kalpas of time. Yet, how does understanding the essential meaning of these scriptures differ from being fully endowed with them?
This merely describes the beginning of practicing for oneself and transforming others.

Regarding the phrase "hearing a single line or a single verse," in general terms, it simply refers to hearing even the most minimal of the Dharma; by citing the profound efficacy of the sutra, it means taking up any single line or verse from within its sections.

In specific terms, it refers here to those instances where the meaning accords with the categories of the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the trace, and the ten wonders and fourfold unities; the merit and blessings are the same in all such cases.

However, since this meaning applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the text below cites the *Ekottarika Āgama* collection, stating, "as with the four noble truths," and further cites the four types of peaceful conduct (*catur-śukla-vihāra*) and so forth; we shall now follow this same principle.

Regarding the statement "all are granted predictions," it is because one must attain Bodhi through this very sutra. Although there may be no difference in the principle of attaining it regardless of the kalpa or realm, here we may employ the intention of "different times. Therefore, one must extensively clarify making offerings by means of hearing and practice, proclaiming and benefiting others, and being fully endowed with internal contemplation, as detailed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Insight).
"How can one simply sit with hands folded and rely solely upon the initial resolve?

As for the phrase 'the middle and superior [capacities] are likewise,' if this were not the case, how could it be that the highest stage belongs to only one person, while those who attain the prediction [of enlightenment] occupy the four stages of the middle?"
It is said that while the teaching is situated here, its application extends to there; therefore, it says, "it is likewise.

Regarding the *Jian shi sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seeing Reality) and so forth: the fourth [chapter] records the eight classes [of beings] first; subsequently, in the fifth fascicle, the "Chapter on the Empty Sky," the empty-walking devas see the various members of the eight classes making offerings and receiving predictions of enlightenment, whereupon they themselves make offerings and all receive predictions, being given the same name, Vahni-dhara.

Next, in the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven," there were eight hundred million gods of the Tuṣita heaven who, seeing the preceding gods receive prophecies through their offerings, likewise all transformed themselves into various articles of worship and simultaneously received prophecies named Indra-dhvaja, preaching the dharma that is like an illusion.

Next, in the "Chapter on the Yāma Heaven," four hundred million Yāma devas also witnessed the devas making offerings and receiving predictions. Having likewise made offerings to the Buddha through miraculous manifestations and by reciting verses, they simultaneously received their predictions, all being named Pure Wisdom (Vimalajñāna).
Regarding the term "Kauśika," it does not appear in that sutra; I suspect it is an error.

As for the "contemplator of the mind," because they penetrate what they recite with the contemplation of the single reality, it is called "one"; there is not a single verse that does not enter into this reality.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," one should clarify the characteristics of a single contemplation; even down to the Master’s method of reciting sutras during contemplation, it is established as a contemplative characteristic by means of recitation and retention—reflect on this carefully.

Regarding "the four exhortations to resolve": first, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, planting the roots of all virtues; third, entering the stage of right determination; and fourth, generating the mind to rescue all sentient beings.

The following text also correlates four dharmas with the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering; although these pertain to the provisional traces (jì), once the fundamental reality (běn) is revealed, they become the essential requirements of that fundamental reality, as will be demonstrated in detail below.
Regarding the statement "the mind of joy is twofold," there are two explanations—horizontal and vertical—and these are further divided into two:
first, the direct explanation; second, the harmonization.
The first [section] itself has two parts:
The initial vertical discussion on rejoicing (*anumodanā*) is divided into three parts:

first, [rejoicing] as the provisional being identical with the real; second, from "At that very moment" (*jia yu*) onwards, the dual negation (*ubhayābhāva*); and third, although this dual negation does not differ from the aforementioned reality, it further enables one to understand that reality is itself the dual negation.

Regarding the initial phrase "in a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*): it does not merely refer to the necessity of passing through a duration of one thought-moment; rather, it points to the dharma of the single mind itself as being called "one thought-moment.

Regarding "believing in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision": within this initial mind, one has deep faith in the wondrous principle. This principle is the object of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; since this object is neither provisional nor ultimate, it is said to be "double negation" (*ubhayābhāva*).
When comparing the principle to hearing, hearing is shallow while the principle is profound; therefore, it is termed "vertical" (*ūrdhva*).
This is the characteristic of the initial stage of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

Third, from "Furthermore, [he] can" onwards, he again illuminates both simultaneously what was previously described as the "double negation"; the perfect fusion of phenomenon and principle is termed the "Secret Treasury."

Although the section "Possessing Afflictions" has not yet entered the formal categories below, it can also serve as a general proof, for it is through the possession of afflictive nature that [the storehouse consciousness] is known.
Furthermore, when comparing the afflictions to the *ālaya*, because the *ālaya* is profound while the afflictions are shallow, it is also termed "vertical."

Next, the section beginning with "Furthermore, if one hears" discusses rejoicing in a horizontal manner; it still points directly toward the non-duality of the provisional and the real, which is why it says "if one hears," and so forth.
The four factors are discussed crosswise to explain sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*): namely, first, the mind; second, the dharma; third, the teaching;
and fourth, the person. Regarding the first, "mind": to regard one's own mind in comparison with other minds is termed "crosswise" (*tiryak*).
In this context, because there is no other mind apart from this single mind, the subsequent text states: "it is horizontal and yet vertical.
As for the phrase "and all dharmas," when all minds are viewed in relation to all dharmas, this is also termed "horizontal."

Because the single mind and the single dharma are both horizontal conditions, the dharma is purely mind and the mind is purely dharma; therefore, the conclusion below states: "The horizontal is precisely the vertical."
Within this context, it is stated that all are the Buddha-dharma; as a matter of principle, the Buddha-dharma is inherently non-dual in its horizontal and vertical dimensions.
The subsequent passage beginning with "If one wishes" explains how the speaker can extensively differentiate each individual mental factor.

Regarding the phrase "from months and four months up to a year," although it cites the passage concerning the faculty of mind (*manas*), this does not yet refer to the stage of the purification of the six faculties; for now, it is explained in terms of contemplation.
The section beginning with "although not yet" can be understood in terms of the practitioner.

Regarding the citation from the Mahāyāna Sūtra: this initial single thought-moment corresponds precisely to "having heard little but understanding much," which is also termed "understanding much while having heard little. Therefore, it is cited here specifically to refute those who, despite their extensive learning, do not understand the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "it shall be explained further later," this occurs in the sixth sutra.
As for the initial mention of "teachers of superior and inferior grades," this is merely a classification based on the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The "ten kinds of offerings" are: first, flowers; second, incense;
third, necklaces; fourth, powdered incense; fifth, unguents; sixth, burning incense; seventh, banners and canopies; eighth, robes; ninth, music; and tenth, joining the palms.
The discussion regarding music is as previously analyzed.

Next, from the passage on the "Medicine King" up to "this person, having abandoned their own purity," [the practitioner] is drawn by the power of compassionate vows; thus, this remains birth through karma (*karmaja*) and has not yet attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This is because the vow is conjoined with karma, as explained in detail in the section on "Retinue" in the *Xuan* (the *Dazhidu lun*). Regarding the phrase "as in the *Śāstra*, there is wisdom but no learning," this verse and the verses on the four Dharma-preachers are fully detailed in the first fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.
Thus, it is known that they also permit the extensive study of divergent doctrines within their own teachings for the sake of propagating the Dharma, so as to assist the orthodox doctrine.
Yet, when people in the world study secular classics and claim they assist the orthodox, they instead sink into the ultimate truth.

Regarding the phrase "It should be known that this person," and so forth: just as a king’s messenger transmits a command, if one accords with the master’s intent, they are called a "messenger" and receive the title of "one who is dispatched.
The initial section beginning with "This sūtra" explains the Tathāgata as the one capable of dispatching; this "one capable of dispatching" refers to the teaching.
Next, from "Today" onwards, the text explains the one who is dispatched; this refers to the person.

From "Performing the work of the Tathāgata" onwards, it explains the task for which he is dispatched. First, the task is explained in terms of his own practice: the Buddha has no other business but to focus exclusively on illuminating the principle (*tattva*).
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "Today," I now perform only the work of the Tathāgata. Suchness (*tathatā*) is the principle (*li*), while its illumination is called the activity (*shi*).

Regarding the section beginning with "The wisdom of such-oneness" (*yīrú zhì*), this is explained in terms of transforming others: the Tathāgata benefits sentient beings through the union of object and wisdom; thus, he takes this very principle and manifests it as a transformative activity. Therefore, we know that great compassion relies upon the illumination of suchness according to the principle, and speaks of suchness according to suchness; this is termed the "activity of the Tathāgata."
"Today," and so forth, refers to performing the Buddha-activities based on this benefit for others.

Regarding the statement, "The Buddha is impartial; evil does not disturb or oppress him," if that were so, there would be no merit in making offerings to the Buddha—why then would one need to make offerings to him?
Question: Since there is no offense in slandering the Buddha, why is it necessary to establish an offense for it?
Answer:
It is indeed so; however, it is done merely to facilitate a comparative analysis.

The previous statement—that regardless of whether a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) is fertile or barren, if one speaks in terms of the field itself, ordinary fields are barren while noble fields are fertile—therefore implies that destroying an offering to a noble field is more serious than to an ordinary one.

Regarding the passage from "For example" to "both are meager," this is also explained in terms of how easily success or failure may occur for a beginner; however, if explained in terms of the field itself, the principle of the analogy can be understood accordingly.

Among the eight fields of merit, nursing the sick is foremost; because many people find it distasteful, the merit of those who do so increases. This is due to the difficulty or ease of the mental state involved.
If one were to judge by the field itself or the nature of the act, how could a single patient ever be compared to the Great Sage or the Sublime Dharma?

It is as if a commoner seeking rescue and a sovereign bestowing gifts were worlds apart; yet the commoner’s gratitude does not conceal itself, while the sovereign’s grace extends to the myriad people. Since the four types of universal benefit must be applied according to what is appropriate, they cannot be standardized by a single rule.
However, this statement can be made because the merit of this sutra is supreme and its principle is peerless;

other sutras are not so. Regarding the phrase "as the shoulder of the Tathāgata" and so forth: the Buddha has attained the provisional, the real, and that which is neither provisional nor real; I too have attained these, and thus it is said that I have attained what the Buddha has attained. This means, in terms of its significance, that [the teaching] rests upon the shoulders and back of the Buddha.

Furthermore, it is because the names of the Buddha’s provisional and ultimate teachings rest upon the shoulders and backs [of sentient beings]; and because sentient beings constantly carry them on their shoulders and backs yet remain unaware of their daily use—whereas other sutras are not so—it is necessary to expound this one.
If it were not so, would those who uphold the sutras all be those upon whose shoulders and backs the Tathāgata carries his burden?
Therefore, this passage must be interpreted by setting aside its literal meaning.

If one is confused regarding the provisional and the real, and the manifestation and the opening [of the truth] in this current text, then even if one applies the names "provisional" and "real" to explain it, one still has not grasped this subtle purport.

Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* that says, "One should hold celestial jewels," and so forth: first, the highest offerings among humans are presented, and subsequently, these are illustrated by way of comparison with celestial jewels.
Since one should even offer celestial jewels, it is said that "one should hold" them.
How much more so for the supreme offerings among humans?
Some say that in the West, whenever something superior is mentioned, it is invariably referred to as "heaven."
If that is so, why was it stated previously that the supreme offerings among humans are themselves divine offerings? Why is this mentioned again?

Regarding the second long prose section, the initial phrase "Praising the Dharma that is upheld" and so forth: the previous passage, concerning the upholder, cited the benefit for others—namely faith and disparagement—to identify the person; this passage, clarifying what is upheld, cites the causes and effects of the person’s state to praise the Dharma.

Within this, first the five chapters are listed, followed by the clarification of their sequential arising; thus, one knows that only when the person, the dharmas, and the locus mutually illuminate one another do they constitute the cause for the production of the fruit.
The phrase "There is a master" below introduces the interpretations of others.
The passage from "The Sūtra praises the Lotus" to "lacking one section" refers to the refutation [of the opponent's view].

This master merely establishes the past and future as the objects of comparison (*prameya*), taking the *Lotus Sūtra* itself as the present subject of comparison (*pramāṇa*). Because this teacher omits the "present" from among the objects of comparison, it is said that "one section" is missing.
The phrase "and so forth" (*yǒuyún*) refers to the explanation of the section on "Manifestation" (*chūxiàn*) based on the following current text. Regarding the phrase "Now, first," and so on:

within this primary explanation, it first enumerates the three periods as being outside the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; subsequently, from the passage "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*" onwards, it clarifies that these three periods do not equal the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, the persons and the Dharma of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are eternally distinct from all other sūtras.
If it were not so, then by refuting and disparaging [the desire for worldly things], the wondrous essence of the *Lotus Sūtra* would be destroyed therein; how then could it constitute a grand eulogy?
This was already the case with Jiaxiang, let alone others.
This refers to passages in texts such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da pin) that, following the sections of the *Xuan* (the *Dazhidu lun*), clarify the five flavors stage by stage.
Were it not for this, how could one know that these had never been explicitly taught from the past?
The secret treasury is not to be given to others recklessly, for it would provoke much resentment and jealousy.

Regarding the term "vanguard": the *Lotus Sūtra* is like a great formation at the front that is difficult to break through, while the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is like the remaining forces at the rear that are not difficult; thus, being the vanguard at the outset is no easy task.

Regarding the passage from "This sutra explains in full" to "is also the secret treasury": the former part reveals the provisional (kaiquan), while the latter part, beginning with "is also," manifests the ultimate reality (xianshi).
Because the provisional is itself the real, it is said that they are "also identical.
Regarding the passage from "Tathāgata" to "enmity and jealousy": reflecting on past evils is termed "enmity," while resenting present goodness is called "jealousy";
thus, those who have not eliminated their faults constitute "enmity," and those who take no pleasure in hearing [the teachings] are named "jealous."

Now, to discuss this comprehensively: in the Trace Gate (Jikimon), the two vehicles and bodhisattvas of dull faculties were envious and jealous; thus, it was not surprising that five thousand people rose and departed.

However, in the Origin Gate (Honmon), those among the bodhisattvas who delight in imminent attainment were envious and jealous; since the entire assembly did not recognize [the Buddha's true nature], how can this be considered strange?
That which remains within the traces can now be seen through its underlying intent.
As for the phrase "the principle is difficult to transform," this clarifies that the purpose of elucidating this principle is to make known that sentient beings are difficult to transform.

Regarding the "four faiths" and the other three powers, the two interpretations in the text together reveal a single underlying meaning: the first correlates them with the three virtues (*triguṇa*), while the second correlates them with the three dharmas. Thus, the four faiths constitute the beginning of practice; the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) serve as the guide; and great wisdom serves as the opener. Therefore, these four faiths must be understood according to the Perfect Vehicle (*yāna*); specifically, when they refer to the Three Jewels of the Single Essence and the ten precepts of a single thought-moment, they alone constitute the foremost of the four great vows within the gateway of the Perfect Teaching.

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Faith means faith in the principle; the principle is the Dharmakāya. If there is a Dharmakāya, then there is the Three Jewels of the single essence of the principle-nature.

Regarding the phrase "aspiration is the establishment of practice," the four great vows establish all practices. The Dharmakāya pertains to that which is believed, while the various practices pertain to that which is induced. Since the root of all wholesome qualities is Prajñā, the four dharmas are fully contained within what is believed.
Since the names are established based on the preeminence of the three qualities, if it were not so, why would he be the object of mindfulness for the Buddhas of this world and other directions?

Regarding the phrase "the initial mind dwells here" and so forth, what is indicated by this usage is as previously described regarding the burden; if it were not so, what benefit would there be in principle for [the Buddha] to cohabit with a physical body or even to touch one's impure head?

Regarding the locations of birth, the attainment of the Way, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and entry into *nirvāṇa*, these are fully detailed in the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mo-ho chih-kuan) concerning the eight manifestations of the *nirmāṇakāya*.

If stupas should be erected at these four sites, how much more so for the five patriarchs and the location of this sutra? These are the four sites of the *dharmakāya*, all of which should have stupas erected; moreover, when the sutra is enshrined within a stupa, it already possesses the whole-body *śarīra* of the *dharmakāya*. Thus, citing the treatises as proof, it is shown that both the *janmakāya* and the *dharmakāya* each possess both whole and fragmented relics.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it causes one to explain the four characteristics: the physical body is completely shattered like that of Śākyamuni or Prabhūtaratna.
As for the two aspects of the *dharmakāya*: in all the teachings of expedient means, the *dharmakāya* is shattered;
in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the single reality, the *dharmakāya* is whole.
The detailed distinctions among the four teachings and five periods can be seen [in other works].

Thus we know that while various sūtras consist of fragments or a mixture of whole and fragmentary parts, only this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the complete body of the Dharmakāya, with no further dharmas remaining, as all enter into reality.
The commentators state:

Previously, taking the person as the fish or the rabbit, [the Buddha's] merit was equated with that of the sixteen-foot [image]; now, taking the words as the trap or the net, they are equal in subtlety to the *śarīra* (relics).

If one does not discriminate between the coarseness or subtlety of its phrasing, and instead equates its merit with that of the physical body, how would this sutra differ from the *Āgamas* or the *Mahāvibhāṣā*?

Thus we know that the commentators did not understand that the "holder" dwells together with the Dharma-Buddha, nor did they realize that what is held is equal to the realm of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya-dhātu). Therefore, among the seventeen names, it is called the "solid relic" (*śarīra*); the "fragmented body" (*kṣetra-śarīra*) does not receive the name "solid."

Regarding "skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*): as explained in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan), which comments on the two degrees of skillfulness and clumsiness, that text from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* generally defines the Mahāyāna gate as skillful; here, however, it specifically designates the One Reality (*eka-yathābhūta*) as skillful.
Regarding the phrase "there are then two kinds," the two texts are first listed; from the words "now it says" onward, the initial meaning is selected for emphasis.
From the words "furthermore, in view of" onward, the proximate essence is explained.
Previously, the provisional [teachings] were designated as "distant" and the perfect [teaching] as "near.

Following this, from the words "Now, by... onwards, the primary intent of the text is explained: taking the single wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) as the cause, one proceeds toward the two fruits of enlightenment—the near and the distant; therefore, the near fruit is elucidated first.

From "the True Suchness prior to the Path" up to "as the efficient cause (pratyaya-hetu)," this means that the cultivated [cause] corresponds to that primary cause (hetu). Within the primary cause itself, the objective condition (ālambana-hetu) and the efficient cause (pratyaya-hetu) together constitute the primary cause; within the cultivation of the primary cause, the primary cause itself constitutes the objective condition and the efficient cause. Regarding the objective condition and efficient cause of the ultimate reality (tathatā), they are also called the "objective condition and efficient cause that are identical with reality," and may also be termed "the objective condition and efficient cause of True Suchness. The principle that the entire nature is cultivation is precisely this meaning.
Only this Dharma is unstained by worldly dharmas; it cannot be destroyed by Māras, nor can it be extinguished by the Two Vehicles, for these reasons.
Thus, taking the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) as the "pre-path" and the period after the arousal of the bodhicitta as the "middle of the path."
Within the stage of the Path (*mārga*), it is divided into two parts:

that prior to the first abiding (*prathama-vihāra*) is the stage of the condition (*pratyaya*), and from the time one has ascended to the abidings onward is the stage of the realization (*phala*). Because a single stage is thus divided into two, it is called "also" (*api*).
The state after the realization of wondrous enlightenment is termed "post-enlightenment" (daohou);
it differs slightly from the preceding stage because the textual passages contrast them.

Within the analogy, one must employ both the two layers of teaching and contemplation to fully exhaust its principle; teaching and contemplation follow one another to jointly manifest its subtlety. If either teaching or contemplation is partial, both will lack efficacy.

First, regarding the section on contemplation (*guan*), the initial part provides a general clarification of contemplation; although the terminology applies broadly to all [teachings], the intent here lies specifically in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

From the phrase "Based on the Contemplation Common to All" (*yi tong guan*) onwards, the contemplations are clarified according to the successive teachings (*jiao*); since the essence and principle sought are identical, the Tripitaka Teaching (*san zang*) is omitted.
Regarding the phrase "the *Dharmapada-śāstra* and so forth," water is like the Buddha-nature; because it is perceived differently [by various beings], it is called "gradual" (*krama*).
That is to say, as the perspectives on the characteristics of the various teachings differ in their depth, one must understand their underlying intent; thus it says, "one should know."

Within the provisional teachings, there are two parts; here too, first there is a general clarification. Below the section on the "Threefold Canon (Tripitaka) Teaching," there is a specific discussion according to the four flavors. Since this treatise discusses the beginning of the gradual teaching, it first presents the Threefold Canon, with the *Avataṃsaka* explained later.

In the previous section on contemplation (*guan*), the four teachings (*sijiao*) were already employed as a framework; therefore, here we further employ the "flavors" (*wei*) to manifest the excellence of the specific divisions (*bu*). The same principle applies if one were to again employ the four teachings within the *Zhi guan*.
In the *Xuán* (Xuanzang’s commentary), all texts first present the four teachings (*sìjiào*).
Next, it cites the *Huáyán* (Avataṃsaka) to verify that the attainment of the waters is identical [to that of the Lotus Sūtra].

Following this, the passage beginning with "There is a person" sets aside the four interpretations of the five schools; three of these schools explain by means of the five periods (*wǔshí*), yet they fail to fully encompass the timeframes and do not follow the correct sequence.

Within the gradual teaching (ānupūrvika-deśanā), the first school discards the first and third [teachings]; the second school discards the first, second, and fourth; and although the third school places the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* after the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, it likewise discards the preceding teachings and thus contradicts the five periods.

Master Daosheng and his commentators have made their determinations entirely based on the *Lotus Sūtra*, yet these are not entirely correct; they have even been refuted by others. Therefore, it is said: "Whether one is far from or near to the Buddha... and so forth.

Thus, the previous three masters share the interpretation that the five periods are used as a single system; the masters Sheng and Zhu likewise share the interpretation that the *Lotus Sūtra* constitutes a single system. Since the present master permits these [interpretations] while refuting their underlying intent, they are recorded here.

The intention of this master is to critique the four interpretations of the previous five masters by dividing them into two categories—the first three and the latter two—and thus refutes them. Regarding the first three, because their various sutras were distant from the Buddha’s time, they all took the Buddha-fruit as "clear water" following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, we know that these three masters were far removed from the Buddha.

Regarding the first interpretation, "near": the latter two masters, based on the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra), define "near" and "far" as beginning from dry earth and ending with clear water, all of which are within the *Lotus Sutra* itself; this is indeed the case if one fundamentally relies on the principles of the True Teaching (*shijiao*).
However, if one contrasts the Real with the Provisional, the principle is not entirely so.

In the section "Examining the Scriptures" below, the Master now synthesizes these views. He notes that the first three masters err because they fail to recognize that the preceding teachings lacked the "pure water," and because their application of the five-period schema all contains minor flaws.

As for the latter two interpretations, they merely discuss proximity and distance within the *Lotus Sūtra* itself; thus, they miss the point of the "opening of the provisional" (*kaikwan*), since everything prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* is precisely what is to be opened.

Now, regarding the Master’s two meanings—those concerning the teachings and those concerning the flavors—the meaning concerning the teachings refers to the three teachings within the previous gradual teaching as being "coarse"; therefore, it is necessary to further explain this solely by means of the Perfect [Teaching] within the Lotus Sūtra.

In terms of the flavors, that which has not yet been transformed among the first four flavors is considered coarse; as for the fifth flavor, although the teaching has already been transformed, practice may not yet have entered it. Therefore, one must provide both distant and proximate interpretations regarding the fifth flavor.
Therefore, it is impossible for either of these two interpretations to be lacking.
Regarding the phrase "The question concerning other sutras," etc., this refers to another person’s inquiry regarding the first of the two preceding interpretations.

Since the previous three masters’ interpretations were judged by others to place the various teachings far removed from the Buddha, the response in the text fully addresses both the distant and the near; accordingly, one should also have asked about both the distant and the near meanings. This is based on those who are exclusively bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles: according to the original intent of the transformation, they originally sought the fruit of Buddhahood, yet because it had not yet been opened up in the past and their provisional capacities had not yet been transformed, it is said that [the matter] was "not yet resolved."
Next, regarding the question, "Why is Prajñāpāramitā distant?"—
since it has been accepted from of old that Prajñā can give rise to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for what reason is it also as distant as the other sūtras?

The meaning of the answer is that, while the general principle is the same as before, it is divided into two senses. First, from the perspective of being common to bodhisattvas yet identical to the two vehicles—before the provisional means (*upāya*) has been revealed—they are said to be far removed from the Buddha.

Next, from the passage "Now, as for Prajñā" onwards, the repeated questions and answers follow in sequence: Prajñā is not distant from the Buddha; since it can give birth to the Dharma-Buddha, how could there be any distance?
This is because it possesses both the provisional and the ultimate wisdoms.
Therefore, an analogy is raised, saying "like a sick person" and so forth.
"The sick person" refers to a bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind toward the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"The two strong men" refers to the two types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because these two types of wisdom lead one to the attainment of Bodhi, it is said that they "can travel everywhere afar.
As for the term "supreme" (*parama*), its meaning lies in its being unshared (*āveṇika*); since this is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is here simply termed "supreme."

Therefore, it is said that the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the provisional (*kaiquan*) is no different from the *Prajñāpāramitā*’s manifestation of the real (*xianshi*). Thus, "revelation of the provisional" and "manifestation of the real" are merely alternative names for the same process; the *Lotus Sūtra* returns to opening up the provisional within the *Prajñāpāramitā* so that it may enter into the reality of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Therefore, it is said that they are not different, yet they are expressed through different names. When discussed in general terms, what distinguishes the *asādhāraṇa-prajñā* (unshared wisdom) from the "seed-wisdom" (*bīja-jñāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
Based on the distinction between being accompanied by [phenomenal attributes] or not, and being opened or not yet opened, there is indeed a difference as well as a similarity.
All the masters fully accord with the present interpretation; therefore, they simply record it directly without offering any refutations.

From the words "Bodhisattva" onwards is the application of the analogy. Since the text already employs the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as its basis for discourse, one may rely on the previous method to provide two interpretations. Regarding why the section explaining the opening of the door of expedient means first extensively cites and examines various points: this is the great purport of the "Trace Gate" (*jitemon*); if this purport were to collapse, by what means could it be propagated?

Regarding this, first the Guangzhai [School] emerged, and subsequently I privately refuted them, stating: "This is a refutation, not an opening. This is because Guangzhai spoke of abolishing the former teachings rather than saying they are identical; therefore, the principle of "opening" (kai) is not established.

Furthermore, because Guangzhai’s words specifically pointed to the Deer Park in the past, we know that interpreting and explaining such statements is no easy task; it is by the single character "remove" (chu) that praise or censure is determined.
Jiaxiang also said:

"Two kinds of skillful means are opened and two kinds of reality are revealed. Previously it was not said that the two were skillful means, and thus the gate was closed; now it is said that the two kinds are skillful means, and thus the gate of skillful means is opened.
While the meaning of opening [the gate] is excellent, establishing [the two as reality] contradicts the teaching.
The Sūtra states: "The Buddha, by the power of skillful means, manifested the teachings of the Three Vehicles. How could it ever have been merely two?
In the present text, even five and seven are all opened up; how then could it be merely three?
However, this is merely a modification of the contemporary literary style, intended to allow later practitioners to employ the terminology without confusion.

Regarding the statement by Hexi, "Directly naming the three as 'expedient means' (upāya)," the meaning is this: in the past, they were called "realities," and since there was no prospect of entering into reality, their gates remained closed;
now, they are termed "expedient means," and because there is hope for advancing toward reality, their gates are said to be opened.

Furthermore, it refers back to the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, which states: "The Buddha, by the power of expedient means, manifests the teachings of the three vehicles. Therefore, Zhiyi (Zhang’an) granted his approval.
Thus, it is truly difficult for ancient scholars to establish their doctrines and adopt [the Mahāyāna] with certainty.
Regarding the statement "twelve and eighty thousand" under the heading "There are people," this refers merely to the twelve divisions and eighty thousand treasuries of the canon.

From the phrase "I privately say" up to "not opening the meaning," [the author] cites the lineage of Master Longshu (Dragon), who followed the distant tradition. Since Master Yin employed both the scriptural teachings and the two kinds of expedient means, we know that he refuted the meaning of [Master Guangzhai’s] illicit appropriation of Longshu’s seal; furthermore, how could his method of using that refutation to explain the "opening of the gate" differ from the meaning of Guangzhai?
Therefore, I shall briefly refute it.
Although this employs the body of the teaching (*śāsana-kāya*), it nonetheless avoids conflating the two [truths].
Regarding the phrase "Questioning the essence of the skillful means," etc., I have provisionally formulated this question in order to引出 (elicit) the subsequent answer.
In my response, I first correctly present two gates; next, from the phrase "these two," I explain that within each of these two gates there is both opening and closing.

Regarding the initial statement "the gate of its own essence" (*dangti*): this has not yet reached the point of universal penetration, as it speaks from outside the essence; rather, it is provisionally called a "gate" because the teachings of this particular school can be entered through it.
If it is said that [this teaching] "is for the sake of the gate of true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is spoken in terms of its ability to lead one to reach true reality.
Regarding the citation of "counting sand to observe the ocean," counting the sand is as explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Fahua Xuanyi*).
Regarding "observing the ocean," the new translation of the sutra, fascicle 67, states:
"There is a city named Kūṭāgāra, in which there is a shipmaster named Bhadra who gathers various merchants and expounds for them all the dharma-gates of the ocean."

Regarding the statement, "These two gates each have their opening and closing": although the essential nature of the dharma-body they access does not differ, they are described according to the perspectives of the past and the present. Thus, what was closed in the past is opened now; the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is likewise so.

Within this, first the essential nature is clarified, followed by the capacity for penetration; these two meanings are each explained in relation to reality (*tattva*), because the true mark (*dharmatā*) likewise possesses both the sense of essential nature and the sense of capacity for penetration.

Although the initial stage within the essence is also called a "gate," it is still closed in reality; therefore, its opening must be clarified. However, while three stages are taught as skillful means, one must be taught as the ultimate truth—this is merely because they are discussed in relation to one another.

The phrase "the second" below next explains the "ability to penetrate," which serves as the gateway to the Real (the *satya*). According to the Buddha’s original intent, both are capable of penetration; however, based on the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, there are two ways they understand it. Even dull-witted bodhisattvas are able to know that the three teachings can penetrate [to the Real], yet before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, their faculties had not yet converged with this truth. Therefore, what was previously closed is now opened simultaneously. For this reason, it is also distinguished in contrast to the Real: how could it be that while the skillful means (*upāya*) are penetrated and the Real is opened, the skillful means remain closed while the True Reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is opened?

Regarding the statement that "this explanation is the same as the two [aspects] of the True Reality (shixiang) of Hexi," it was previously addressed directly in relation to the skillful means; now, it is discussed in detail because it is identical to those skillful means, hence the word "also" (yi).

Regarding "pervasive penetration" (*kūtsū*): this explains that the reality itself constitutes the gate. Being unobstructed is called "void" (*kū*), and being without impediment is called "penetration" (*tsū*). Thus, the entire substance becomes a gate capable of penetrating; it contains all things without any separation or obstruction, thereby earning the name "gate. Since there is nowhere throughout all places that is not a gate, this is a case where, regarding the reality, there is no penetration yet there is penetration. Therefore, it is termed "non-duality" (*funi*) and "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*). The Dharma-realm itself is the gate, thus it is called the "Dharma-realm Gate"; this is not like a gate made of counting-sand, which is a gate as a mere physical entity.

Second, regarding "the gate of skillful means that enables penetration": it is called "enabling penetration" because it causes skillful means to reach the ultimate reality. If it were not for the power of the true mark (*dharmatā*), there would be no way for skillful means to open. Thus, we know that the single principle of ultimate reality receives its name from these two [aspects]. Because it is empty and penetrating, it allows others to take refuge; it is like a general amnesty whose substance pervades all, so that there is no crime that is not pardoned.

Regarding the meaning of "Liu Qiu": the first phrase correctly clarifies that reality serves as the gateway for the provisional; the second phrase clarifies that the three kinds of provisionality serve as the gateway for reality; and the words "not three" and following clarify that these two gateways open into one another.

Thus, Liu Qiu was not unwilling to provide private commentaries on the *Shenghui*, but his language was concise and his meaning profound, making it difficult for the essential purport of the sutra to be revealed.
Someone said:

"Others establish three chapter-headings, each serving as a skillful means for the others and each functioning as a gateway; however, compared to the commentators [of the *Shenghui*], their wording is excessively verbose and their principles are chaotic. Although they speak much, they have little substance; it is better to adhere to the One."

Within this, first the items are listed; next, from "Just as... onwards, they are explained. This explains the intention behind the three turnings of the wheel according to the Five Periods school within the "Expedient Means" (Upāya) chapter.

The only difference lies in the fact that [the other two chapters] are presented as mutual gateways, whereas this one alone is explained as the first chapter; the remaining two are merely listed. The intent of the first chapter is that [the provisional teachings] were established because sentient beings' minds were obstructed; now that the provisional has been opened, it is called "penetration" (*tong*).
In reality, there is fundamentally no threefold [nature], yet it appears as three for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is said that they "arise.

Regarding the remaining two examples following the phrase "even unto," first there is the illustration, and next, from the words "but one cannot" onwards, the meaning of the text concerning its pervasiveness and obstructions is explained.

If one wishes to set forth a second example: just as taking "three-and-one" (*tri-eka*) serves as the gateway to that which is neither three nor one—since by realizing "three-and-one," one reaches the state of dual negation (*ubhaya-abhāva*), and because from dual negation "three-and-one" arises—therefore, "neither-three-nor-one" serves as the gateway to "three-and-one."
The third case, by analogy, should also be understood in this way.

Next, regarding the principles of pervasion and obstruction: if one is able to pervade and give rise to [the teaching], one may discuss the gates interchangeably; however, one must not take one as provisional and the three as real. To employ the text of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in that manner is not the intended meaning here.
The same applies to the latter two chapters, though they function as gates for one another.

In the subsequent "Private Refutation," only the first chapter is refuted; the remaining two are treated by analogy with the first. Within the first chapter, only the three [aspects] being unified into a single gate is refuted, while the one [aspect] being divided into three gates has not yet been refuted.

The initial text has two layers: first, the refutation of the meaning of the "gate" (dvāra); second, the refutation by means of its not being a cause (*ahetu*). Regarding the meaning of the first gate:

the first phrase establishes that within concentration (*samādhi*), only the three [mental] applications (*manasikāra*) correspond to a single phrase; this refutes the meaning of the gate, using their lack of mutual correspondence as the obstruction, so that they naturally cease to be a gate. Furthermore, one should also say:
"If they were mutually correspondent, why did they not correspond in the past, such that they would persist until the present?"
What was previously inaccessible was not a gate in the past.
"If it is opened" and so forth, down to the present, it is precisely this that is opened; once opened, it is no longer three. How can one take those three as a single gate of entry?
This reveals that others do not understand what is internal and what is external; therefore, it must be dismantled.
According to the Buddha’s original intent, it was fundamentally intended for universal penetration; thus, before it was opened, it was inherently a gateway.
Since he has not yet stated that it is "opened" to call it a "gate," it must be refuted.
Thus we know that even for three to constitute a single gate, it is already untenable; what need is there to separately refute one being three gates?
If that is so, why does the *Sūtra* say, "Opening the gate of skillful means"?
Answer:
From our current perspective, although the gate has not yet been opened, it is still called a "gate" in the sense that it is capable of being opened.
Just as this is fundamentally a door, when it is closed, is it not still a door?
It is merely called a "closed door.
Once opened, the three [distinctions] no longer exist; why, then, should it hinder us from taking the three as the door from of old?
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, three are not causes for Buddhahood," the intent of the refutation is the same as before.
If even when unopened they are not causes individually, how much more so when they have been opened, yet remain in a distracted state of mind?
Next, the refutation of the remaining two [chapters] follows the same pattern as the first; this should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yǒuyún*): if one were to provide a detailed refutation of the first chapter, it would be too cumbersome to describe in full the subsequent half-chapter—which treats the real as a provisional gate—and the following two chapters, as their meaning is thin and the details are overly intricate.

Once he has been refuted, one may now establish two further propositions based on this; since his refutation is complete, the establishment of one's own position follows naturally, as explained in detail previously.

Regarding the phrase "Inquiring into the Expedient Means" (*upāya*), this question is posed now in order to open up the thematic scope of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Thus, since the Master’s preceding text already contains two propositions, can the remaining two propositions also be formulated?

The passage beginning with "This exists" provides the answer in four propositions; the latter two propositions have no distinct meaning in principle, but are merely presented through names and meanings to explain the characteristics of the propositions.

Within this, first the preceding two [points] are indicated, followed by the listing of the latter two phrases. Third, under the heading "As with names," etc., examples are cited to provide an explanation; first the names and their meanings are listed, and then, under "By means of skillful methods," etc., they are explained by way of example. Since meaning is the intended purport underlying a name, these two may serve as gates for one another.
Within this, first the "expedient means" (upāya) is explained; next, from the section on "true reality" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) onwards, it is explained by way of analogy.

First comes the analogy, followed by the citation of scriptural evidence from the "Introduction to the Madhyamaka-śāstra. Here, the name "reality" and the meaning "reality" serve as mutual gateways for one another.
"Reality" (shí) is the meaning;
"Middle" (zhōng) is the name.
Thus, by employing the name "Middle" to manifest the meaning of "Middle," this constitutes the "gate of meaning through names."

The text mentions only one side; it should also state that "it is also by virtue of the real object (*vastu*) being able to correspond to the name. Since a name cannot be established without a real object, the real object is cited here to lead [the understanding] toward it.

Regarding the statement, "The question asks how the three are manifested by means of the three," and so forth: since the provisional (upāya) and the ultimate (tattva) are themselves but the three and the one, and since the provisional and the ultimate already constitute four propositions (catuṣkoṭi), does it follow by analogy that the three and the one likewise possess the latter two [propositions]?
The section beginning with "This also" provides the answer.
Regarding the statement "the two are as before": three being treated as one gate is like using three to manifest one; one being treated as three gates is like using one to manifest three.

The phrase "using three to manifest three" explains the latter two lines. Since the former two lines already used the triads of name, meaning, and characteristics to mutually manifest the provisional and the real, the latter two lines cannot employ name and meaning for their explanation as they did previously;
rather, they are explained solely by means of the mutual correspondence of the essential natures (*dharmatā*) themselves.

Within this, there are three parts: first, the preliminary explanation; second, the formal judgment and conclusion beginning with "Since the three and the one are neither..."; and third, the manifestation of the relationship between cultivation and nature beginning with "By means of causes and conditions..."
The first section also has two parts: the heading and the explanation.
In the initial text, there is only the heading of one phrase, with the phrase "to manifest by means of one" omitted.
From the words "As for 'of old'" (*yán xī*) onwards, the explanation fully contains both phrases, which further divides into two parts:
First, the errors are pointed out; next, from "Refuting This" onwards, is the formal explanation.
Regarding the initial pointing out of the errors: this is done by way of an introductory exposition to refute the notion that the present and the past are different.

Within this, first the characteristics of the error are presented: if even the mutual interpenetration of the three and the one cannot be established, how much less can the three be used to manifest the three, or the one to manifest the one?
The phrase "Therefore, one" below concludes the refutation.

Regarding the statement "One is not three, nor three one," etc., since the one and the three are neither identical nor mutually exclusive, if they were not opened up [as distinct], their mutual manifestation could not be established; thus, the one is not the one of the three houses, and the three are not the three of the one house.

Next, from "Refuting This" onwards, the text provides a formal explanation based on the present sutra. First, it cites the passage "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, they differentiate and teach three," to prove that the three are identical to the one; next, it cites "The path you practice is the bodhisattva path," to prove that the one is identical to the three. Thus, the bestowing of the one and the three, and the one within the three, constitutes the "three-and-one" that opens up the three to reveal the one.

The first phrase refers back to the past, hence it says, "distinctly teaching three"; the second phrase reveals the present, hence it says, "this is the path of the bodhisattva. Because the former teachings had not yet been revealed, the three and the one were still separated; thus it was not said that the manifestation of the three is the one, nor that the one is the three, nor that the three and the one are identical to the one and the three.

Since it has now been stated that there is no "three" apart from the "one," these three constitute the three of this single school; that is, the "three" previously existing apart from the "one" have become entirely the three of this single school. Therefore, it is said: "By means of the three, the three are revealed."

Once the one is opened and established, there is no "one" outside the three; it is thus one of the three families. That is to say, the "one" that was previously outside the three now fully becomes one of the three; therefore, it is said, "the one reveals the one."

Therefore, we know that by means of the three manifested externally to the substance, the one is manifested as the three; and by means of the one manifested externally to the three, the three are manifested as the one.

Next, from the passage beginning "Since the three and the one are neither... onwards is the judgment and conclusion. This is intended to introduce the subsequent discussion on the three and the one of causes and conditions; therefore, it is judged first.
Regarding the statement that "the three and the one are not mutually distinct," this judges that what was previously revealed belongs entirely to the realm of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
What is termed "causes and conditions" refers precisely to the ritual manifestations of response and resonance (*ganying*), which are also called "cultivated attainment."
Third, from "by means of causes and conditions" onwards, there is the combined discernment of cultivation and nature.

As for "intrinsic nature," it refers to the qualities of nature; thus, although the threefold unity of the qualities of nature is primordially present—neither cultivated nor contrived—it manifests through causes and conditions as the one within the three, thereby revealing that the qualities of nature are the one within the three.

Furthermore, because the qualities of nature (xingde) are three yet one, the causal conditions that enable [awakening] are one among those three; likewise, because the causal conditions are one yet three, they manifest the three within the oneness of the qualities of nature.
Furthermore, by virtue of the three within the one of the inherent qualities (*dharmatā-guṇa*), the causes and conditions that can bestow [these qualities] are precisely the three within the one.
Thus, the causes and conditions are the one within the three, and the manifestation of self-nature is the one within the three; this is termed "manifesting the one by means of the one.
Because the causes and conditions are the three within the one, and the manifestation of self-nature is the three within the one, it is termed "manifesting the three by means of the three."
The nature reveals the conditions; this can be understood by applying the same principle.
Regarding the mutual appearance of the three and one in the concluding passage, it is because they mutually reveal one another, rather than not doing so.

To reveal the three by means of the three is simply to reveal the one by means of the three; to reveal the one by means of the one is simply to reveal the three by means of the one. Although these explanations resolve difficulties and exhaustively reach the source, if one studies the teachings of this school and remains confused about this principle, one will merely waste mental energy.

Regarding the citation of the fifteen gateways of illumination (*vidyā-mukha*): although their number is listed, one still does not know which among them must be opened, which have already been opened, or what the characteristics of these gateways are.
If it is not so determined, what benefit is there in merely listing them?

According to the intent of the present text, all that is provisional within the fifteen gates must be opened up; as is fully explained in the commentary on each passage, anything therein that contradicts our current interpretation should also be refuted. For example, when the *Upāya-paryāya* chapter cites "wisdom" as a gate, this refers to the provisional wisdom that is identical in essence [to ultimate reality]; how could it be said that this serves as a gate for the sake of the Real?
Next is the "Various Gates"; since these are provisional gates, why speak only of the Mahāyāna teachings?
Following this, from "There is only one gate" onwards, the focus is no longer exclusively on the teachings.
Regarding the phrase "the gates of what is burned delimit the three realms," how could it be said that [the fire] merely emerges from those boundaries?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the chariot is outside the gates and refers to the three realms," the refutation is likewise as before.

The "Lesser Teaching" serves as the gateway, yet it does not yet distinguish between those who have undergone cremation and so forth; thus, standing outside the gate, it is divided into two interpretations. These state that while the exhaustion of formal practice exists only within the general sense of the gateway, those on the side of the gate—if they were Mahāyāna practitioners—should already have attained the Mahāyāna. To remain still outside the gate as before would be inconsistent with both of the preceding interpretations.

Regarding the phrase "inside the gate as before," the meaning is the same as being outside the gate previously; whereas one was previously outside the gates of the two deaths, now one must not remain within those two deaths.

Regarding the phrase "Opening the Gate of Ambrosia, called Great or Small," this is the text of the invitation by the Brahmās of the ten directions; it may indeed be like this, yet I do not know where it currently resides, nor whether it belongs to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna teachings.

The meaning of the present text is that it fundamentally aims to open the gates, not to enumerate them; it fundamentally aims to explain the gates, not to know their number. If one were to enumerate and simplify them, what fault would there be in simplifying those gates already opened?

The passage beginning with "In the past, it was said that all worlds... further cites the faculty of mind (*manas*) to clarify and reveal its meaning. This serves to open up the various categories enumerated by ancient masters; for even the means of livelihood (*upajīvana*) from the past were not yet considered expedient means (*upāya*), yet now that they have been revealed, they are seen to be entirely true—how much more so, then, the case of the three vehicles and five vehicles?

Regarding the phrase "whether a gate or not a gate": that which is "not a gate" refers to the principles and teachings of the Hīnayāna, such as form, fragrance, and the necessities of life; that which is "a gate" refers to the two contemplations of the Distinct Teaching (Bie-jiao) serving as skillful means. Because these were taught from the beginning, there are gates and non-gates; however, at this present stage, everything is universally accessible and nothing is not a gate.

Regarding "exhortation to practice": because one dwells in the three dharmas and still exhorts others not to be indolent before subsequently speaking from the heart, it is known that this refers only to the first two stages within the position of contemplative practice (vipaśyanā-caryā).

Therefore, one encourages the propagation of the Perfect Sūtra to benefit others; yet when the merit of this transformation is attributed to oneself upon reaching the stage of "Similarity," the wondrous voice spontaneously pervades the three thousandfold world-systems without waiting for further exhortation.
Among these, the three dharmas are each said to possess the other three in mutual relation: first, compassion and loving-kindness are indicated; next, from "If one considers...

onwards, it clarifies that each one contains the three; then, from "Cultivating the Tathāgata... onwards, gentleness is indicated; next, from "If one considers... onwards, it clarifies that each one contains the three; and finally, from "If one considers those who are seated... onwards, there is no specific indication, as it directly clarifies the three within *prajñā*. Although each possesses [the others], they are merely a single triad; since even three are not truly three, how could they be divided into nine?
This means that the bodhisattva constantly contemplates nirvana; therefore, he exhorts those who propagate the sutra to do the same.
May those who propagate the sutra contemplate it as they propagate it—for how can one understand the principle being propagated without contemplating the mind that propagates it?
Therefore, the Buddha allows those who enter my chamber, wear my robes, and sit upon my seat; if they lack these three dharmas, how can they be said to propagate the sutra?

In the section on "Peaceful Practices" (*Anle-xing*), the text from the lower fascicle is cited, which likewise possesses this benefit; thus, it is urged that those who propagate the teaching should rely upon the prescribed methods.
The phrase "the preceding text" refers to the citation of the aforementioned passage below to provide an explanation and establish the point.
Regarding the "five matters," they are the same five items listed previously under the section on benefits, beginning with the first: the dispatching of emanated persons, and so forth.
